gelu  = lambda x: 0.5 * x * (1 + np.tanh(0.797 * (x + 0.044 * x**3)))
silu  = lambda x: x / (1 + np.exp(-x))
sections.caption: Different shapes near zero, same job: inject nonlinearity.

takeaways: Activations make a deep stack more than one linear layer.
ReLU keeps gradients alive through depth.
GELU/SiLU are smooth variants common in transformers.

concepts.title: Backpropagation
concepts.oneLine: Get the gradient for every parameter in one backward pass.

paras: Backprop is the chain rule run efficiently over the whole network. A forward pass computes the output and caches intermediate values; a backward pass sends the error signal from the loss back through each layer, accumulating the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight in a single sweep.
The error signal at a layer propagates through the local Jacobian:
sections.texNote: Then the weight gradient is delta times the layer's input - reuse, not recompute.

sections.code:
# backward through one ReLU layer
dZ = dA * (Z > 0)            # gradient through ReLU
dW = dZ @ A_prev.T           # weight gradient
dA_prev = W.T @ dZ           # pass the signal down
sections.caption: One backward sweep yields every gradient at once.

takeaways: Backprop is reverse-mode automatic differentiation.
One forward + one backward pass gives all gradients.
It reuses cached activations instead of recomputing.

concepts.title: Batch Normalization
concepts.oneLine: Normalize activations across the batch to stabilize training.

paras: As signals pass through layers, their scale can drift and stall learning. Batch norm renormalizes each feature to zero mean and unit variance over the mini-batch, then lets the network rescale with learned parameters. It smooths the loss landscape, allows higher learning rates, and adds a little regularizing noise.
Standardize over the batch, then shift and scale:
sections.texNote: gamma and beta are learned; at inference, running statistics replace the batch ones.

sections.code:
mu = x.mean(0); var = x.var(0)
xhat = (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + 1e-5)
y = gamma * xhat + beta
sections.caption: Standardize per feature, then let the net rescale.

takeaways: Batch norm keeps activation statistics stable across depth.
It enables higher learning rates and faster convergence.
Layer norm is the batch-free variant used in transformers.

concepts.title: The Multilayer Perceptron
concepts.oneLine: Stack linear layers and nonlinearities into a universal function approximator.

paras: A multilayer perceptron alternates two operations: a linear map (weights and a bias) and a per-neuron nonlinearity. Without the nonlinearity, stacking layers collapses to a single linear map; with it, a wide-enough network can approximate any continuous function.
Each layer applies a weight matrix, a bias, and an activation:
sections.texNote: Depth composes simple features into complex ones; the nonlinearity is what makes depth matter.

sections.caption: Linear, nonlinear, repeat - then a final linear head.

takeaways: An MLP is alternating linear maps and nonlinearities.
The nonlinearity is what makes depth more than one big linear layer.
Wide enough, it can approximate any continuous function.

concepts.title: Optimizers: SGD to Adam
concepts.oneLine: Turn raw gradients into stable, fast parameter updates.

paras: Plain SGD takes a fixed step against the gradient. Momentum smooths the path by accumulating a velocity; Adam goes further, keeping per-parameter running averages of the gradient and its square so each weight gets its own adaptive step size. Adam is the default for most deep learning.
Adam rescales each step by a running estimate of the gradient and its magnitude:
sections.texNote: m is the momentum (first moment), v the per-parameter scale (second moment).

sections.code:
m = beta1*m + (1-beta1)*g
v = beta2*v + (1-beta2)*g*g
mh, vh = m/(1-beta1**t), v/(1-beta2**t)
theta -= lr * mh / (np.sqrt(vh) + 1e-8)
sections.caption: Momentum plus per-parameter scaling - the Adam update.

takeaways: Momentum smooths noisy gradients into a steadier path.
Adam gives each parameter its own adaptive step size.
It is the safe default for most deep networks.

concepts.title: Weight Initialization
concepts.oneLine: Start with the right variance so signals neither vanish nor explode.

paras: If initial weights are too small, activations shrink to nothing through depth; too large, and they blow up. Good initialization sets the variance so the signal's scale is preserved layer to layer. Xavier targets this for tanh, He for ReLU.
He initialization scales by the fan-in for ReLU networks:
sections.texNote: The 2 compensates for ReLU zeroing half the activations.

sections.code:
import numpy as np
# He init for a ReLU layer
W = np.random.randn(n_out, n_in) * np.sqrt(2.0 / n_in)
sections.caption: Set the variance to keep signal scale constant through depth.

takeaways: Initialization controls whether deep signals vanish or explode.
Xavier suits tanh; He suits ReLU.
It matters most before normalization layers are added.

concepts.title: Convolutional Networks
concepts.oneLine: Stack convolutions and pooling into a hierarchy of visual features.

paras: A CNN interleaves convolutions (detect features) with pooling (shrink and gain invariance), building a hierarchy from edges to textures to object parts. The final feature map feeds a classifier or a detector head. This inductive bias - locality and weight sharing - is what makes vision models data-efficient.
Pooling downsamples a region to one value, e.g. the max:
sections.texNote: Each conv-pool stage widens the receptive field and adds translation invariance.

sections.caption: Conv to detect, pool to summarize - repeat, then classify.

takeaways: CNNs build a feature hierarchy via conv + pool stages.
Locality and weight sharing make them data-efficient on images.
Detection and segmentation reuse the same backbone.

concepts.title: Convolution
concepts.oneLine: Slide a small learnable kernel over the input to detect local patterns.

paras: A convolution slides a small filter across the image, computing a weighted sum at every position. Because the same weights are reused everywhere, the layer detects a pattern (an edge, a texture) wherever it appears, with far fewer parameters than a dense layer. Stacking convolutions builds from edges to objects.
Each output pixel is a dot product of the kernel with a local patch:
sections.texNote: Weight sharing gives translation equivariance and parameter efficiency.

sections.caption: One kernel, reused at every position.

takeaways: Convolution applies a shared filter across all positions.
Weight sharing gives translation equivariance and few parameters.
Stacked convolutions grow from edges to objects.

concepts.title: Data Augmentation
concepts.oneLine: Manufacture label-preserving variety to regularize a vision model.

paras: A flipped, rotated, or cropped cat is still a cat. Augmentation applies these label-preserving transforms during training so the model sees far more variety than the raw dataset holds, teaching invariance to nuisance factors and curbing overfitting - the cheapest regularizer in vision.
Train on transformed inputs whose label is unchanged:
sections.texNote: T is sampled fresh each epoch; the family T encodes which variations should not change the label.

sections.code:
import numpy as np

def augment(img):
    if np.random.rand() < 0.5: img = img[:, ::-1]      # h-flip
    img = np.roll(img, np.random.randint(-3, 4), axis=0) # shift
    return img
sections.caption: Fresh random transforms each epoch multiply the effective data.

takeaways: Augmentation adds label-preserving variety for free.
It teaches invariance and reduces overfitting.
Strong augmentation underpins modern self-supervised vision.

concepts.title: LSTM Gates
concepts.oneLine: Gates let a recurrent net keep or forget information over long spans.

paras: The LSTM adds a cell state that information can travel along nearly untouched, controlled by gates: a forget gate decides what to drop, an input gate what to add, an output gate what to expose. This gated highway keeps gradients alive far longer than a plain RNN.
Each gate is a learned sigmoid; the cell is updated additively:
sections.texNote: The additive update is what preserves gradient flow across many steps.

sections.code:
f = sigmoid(Wf @ z)    # forget
i = sigmoid(Wi @ z)    # input
o = sigmoid(Wo @ z)    # output
c = f * c + i * np.tanh(Wc @ z)
h = o * np.tanh(c)
sections.caption: Gates throttle what the cell keeps, adds, and reveals.

takeaways: LSTM gates control keep / add / expose for the cell state.
The additive cell update fights vanishing gradients.
GRUs are a lighter, two-gate variant.

concepts.title: Markov Chains
concepts.oneLine: Model a sequence where the next step depends only on the current state.

paras: A Markov chain assumes the future depends on the present, not the full past. n-gram language models are exactly this: predict the next token from the last few. It is a weak assumption that is still a surprisingly strong baseline - and the conceptual ancestor of every sequence model.
The Markov property drops all but the current state:
sections.texNote: Transition probabilities are just normalized counts of observed pairs.

sections.caption: Count pairs, normalize, sample - an n-gram model.

takeaways: Markov models condition only on the current state.
n-gram language models are Markov chains over tokens.
They are a strong, simple baseline for sequences.

concepts.title: Recurrent Networks
concepts.oneLine: Carry a hidden state across time to model sequences of any length.

paras: An RNN reads a sequence one step at a time, updating a hidden state that summarizes everything seen so far. The same weights apply at every step, so it handles arbitrary lengths. It was the pre-transformer way to model order - but long-range dependencies are hard because gradients vanish through time.
The hidden state recurs through a shared cell:
sections.texNote: Trained by backprop through time; repeated multiplication makes gradients vanish or explode.

sections.caption: One shared cell, unrolled over the sequence.

takeaways: RNNs maintain a running summary in a hidden state.
Shared weights handle variable-length input.
Vanishing gradients limit their memory - which LSTMs address.

concepts.title: Word2Vec
concepts.oneLine: Learn word vectors by predicting a word from its context.

paras: Words that appear in similar contexts should have similar vectors. Skip-gram trains embeddings by pushing a word's vector toward the words around it and away from random negatives. The result is the famous geometry where king - man + woman lands near queen.
Skip-gram maximizes the probability of context given the center word:
sections.texNote: Negative sampling approximates the costly denominator with a few random words.

sections.code:
# one skip-gram step with negative sampling
score = v_center @ v_context
grad = (sigmoid(score) - label) * v_center   # label 1 for true ctx, 0 for neg
v_context -= lr * grad
sections.caption: Pull true context together, push negatives apart.

takeaways: Distributional meaning: context predicts the embedding.
Negative sampling makes training cheap.
It produces vectors with linear analogy structure.

concepts.title: Attention
concepts.oneLine: Weight every token by how relevant it is to the one you are computing.

paras: Attention lets each token pull in information from every other token, weighted by relevance. Each token emits a query (what am I looking for?), a key (what do I offer?), and a value (what I'll pass along). A token's output is a relevance-weighted average of everyone's values.
This is the operation that replaced recurrence: instead of passing a state step by step, every token talks to every other token in one parallel step.
Scaled dot-product attention scores each query against every key, softmax-normalizes the scores into weights, and mixes the values. The 1/sqrt(d_k) keeps the dot products from saturating the softmax:
sections.texNote: Q, K, V are linear projections of the input. See the full derivation in the on-site Self-Attention lesson.

sections.code:
import numpy as np

def attention(Q, K, V):
    dk = Q.shape[-1]
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(dk)     # (n, n) relevance
    scores -= scores.max(-1, keepdims=True)
    w = np.exp(scores)
    w /= w.sum(-1, keepdims=True)      # softmax over keys
    return w @ V                       # weighted mix of values
sections.caption: Three matmuls and a softmax — the core of every transformer.

takeaways: Attention is a content-based, weighted average of values — no recurrence required.
Queries and keys decide the weights; values carry the information.
The sqrt(d_k) scaling keeps gradients healthy as the dimension grows.

concepts.title: Decoding
concepts.oneLine: Turn the model's next-token distribution into actual generated text.

paras: A language model outputs a probability distribution over the next token. Decoding is the policy that picks one — and that choice shapes everything about the output. Always taking the argmax (greedy) is fluent but repetitive; sampling adds variety but can wander.
Temperature sharpens or flattens the distribution; top-k and top-p (nucleus) clip the long tail so you sample only from plausible tokens; beam search keeps several candidate continuations at once.
Temperature T rescales the logits before the softmax — low T concentrates probability on the top tokens, high T spreads it out:
sections.texNote: T -> 0 recovers greedy argmax; T = 1 is the model's raw distribution.

sections.code:
import numpy as np

def sample(logits, T=1.0, top_p=0.9):
    z = logits / T
    p = np.exp(z - z.max()); p /= p.sum()
    order = np.argsort(p)[::-1]                 # nucleus: keep smallest
    keep = order[np.cumsum(p[order]) <= top_p]  # set with mass >= top_p
    if len(keep) == 0: keep = order[:1]
    p2 = p[keep] / p[keep].sum()
    return np.random.choice(keep, p=p2)
sections.caption: Temperature reshapes the distribution; top-p trims the tail before sampling.

takeaways: Decoding is a separate policy on top of the model's distribution — it controls the style of the output.
Temperature trades determinism for diversity; top-k / top-p remove implausible tokens.
Greedy is just temperature -> 0; beam search searches several continuations at once.

concepts.title: Embeddings
concepts.oneLine: Map each token id to a dense vector whose geometry carries meaning.

paras: A token id is just an index — id 4017 means nothing on its own. An embedding layer is a learned lookup table that turns each id into a vector of real numbers, and training shapes that table so related tokens land near each other.
Once tokens are vectors, 'meaning' becomes geometry: similarity is a dot product, analogies are directions, and every later layer gets to do linear algebra instead of string matching.
The embedding matrix is E in R^(V x d) for vocabulary size V and model width d. Looking up token i is just selecting a row:
sections.texNote: E is a parameter — it is learned by gradient descent like any other weight.

sections.code:
import numpy as np

V, d = 50000, 256
E = np.random.randn(V, d) * 0.02      # learned embedding table

ids = np.array([101, 4017, 2009])     # a tokenized sentence
x = E[ids]                            # (3, d) — one vector per token

# similarity between two tokens is a dot product
cos = E[4017] @ E[2009] / (np.linalg.norm(E[4017]) * np.linalg.norm(E[2009]))
sections.caption: The whole layer is a row-select; the magic is in what training writes into E.

takeaways: Embeddings convert discrete ids into a continuous space where similarity is measurable.
The table is learned, so structure (synonyms, analogies) emerges from the training objective.
Every downstream layer benefits — they all operate on vectors, never on tokens.

concepts.title: Multi-Head Attention
concepts.oneLine: Run several attention patterns in parallel, then combine them.

paras: One attention map forces every token to mix information in a single way. Real language needs several relationships at once — syntactic agreement, coreference, local phrasing. Multi-head attention splits the model width into h smaller subspaces, runs attention independently in each, and concatenates the results.
Each head is cheap (it works in d/h dimensions), and together they let the layer attend to different things in different subspaces simultaneously.
Each head projects Q, K, V into its own subspace, attends there, and the outputs are concatenated and mixed by a final projection W^O:
sections.texNote: head_i = Attention(XW_i^Q, XW_i^K, XW_i^V); the heads run fully in parallel.

sections.code:
import numpy as np

def multi_head(X, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, h):
    n, d = X.shape
    dk = d // h
    outs = []
    for i in range(h):                 # each head sees a d/h slice
        sl = slice(i * dk, (i + 1) * dk)
        outs.append(attention(X @ Wq[:, sl], X @ Wk[:, sl], X @ Wv[:, sl]))
    return np.concatenate(outs, axis=-1) @ Wo
sections.caption: Heads are independent; the final W^O lets them interact.

takeaways: Multiple heads capture multiple relationships in parallel subspaces.
Splitting the width keeps the total cost the same as single-head attention.
The output projection W^O lets the heads' results recombine.

concepts.title: Positional Encoding
concepts.oneLine: Inject order into a model that otherwise treats its input as a set.

paras: Attention has no built-in notion of order — shuffle the tokens and the raw computation is unchanged. But language is sequential: 'dog bites man' is not 'man bites dog'. Positional encodings add a position-dependent signal to each token vector so the model can tell where each token sits.

The classic transformer uses fixed sinusoids of geometrically increasing wavelength. Because sines and cosines combine linearly, the model can represent relative offsets — a useful inductive bias that also extends to lengths never seen in training.
For position pos and dimension i, the encoding interleaves sine and cosine across a spectrum of frequencies:
sections.texNote: Added to the token embedding before the first attention layer.

sections.code:
import numpy as np

def positional_encoding(seq_len, d):
    pos = np.arange(seq_len)[:, None]
    i = np.arange(d)[None, :]
    angle = pos / np.power(10000, (2 * (i // 2)) / d)
    pe = np.where(i % 2 == 0, np.sin(angle), np.cos(angle))
    return pe                          # (seq_len, d), add to embeddings
sections.caption: Different dimensions oscillate at different rates — a positional fingerprint.

takeaways: Self-attention is permutation-invariant; position must be added explicitly.
Sinusoidal encodings let the model reason about relative position and generalize past trained lengths.
Modern variants (RoPE, ALiBi) encode position inside attention instead of adding it up front.

concepts.title: Tokenization
concepts.oneLine: Turn raw text into the discrete tokens a model actually consumes.

paras: A language model never sees characters or words — it sees a sequence of integer token ids drawn from a fixed vocabulary. Tokenization is the step that converts a string into that sequence, and back.

Word-level vocabularies explode and choke on typos and rare words; character-level keeps the vocabulary tiny but makes sequences painfully long. Subword tokenization (BPE, WordPiece, Unigram) is the compromise everyone uses: common words stay whole, rare ones split into reusable pieces, and nothing is ever out-of-vocabulary.

Byte-Pair Encoding learns its vocabulary greedily. Start from single characters, then repeatedly merge the adjacent pair with the highest frequency across the corpus until you hit the target vocabulary size:
sections.texNote: Each chosen pair becomes a new token; the merge list, applied in order, is the tokenizer.

sections.code:
from collections import Counter

# greedy BPE merge step over a corpus of symbol-lists
def best_pair(corpus):
    pairs = Counter()
    for word in corpus:                # word = ['l','o','w','</w>']
        for a, b in zip(word, word[1:]):
            pairs[(a, b)] += 1
    return pairs.most_common(1)[0][0]  # the pair to merge next

def merge(corpus, pair):
    a, b = pair
    return [_join(word, a, b) for word in corpus]
sections.caption: Run best_pair -> merge in a loop until the vocabulary reaches the size you want.

takeaways: Models operate on token ids, not text — tokenization defines what a 'unit' even is.
Subword tokenizers trade vocabulary size against sequence length and eliminate out-of-vocabulary words.
BPE is just: merge the most frequent adjacent pair, repeat.

concepts.title: The Transformer Block
concepts.oneLine: Stack attention and an MLP with residuals and normalization into one repeatable unit.

paras: A transformer is just the same block stacked many times. Each block does two things: mix information across tokens (attention), then transform each token on its own (a small MLP). Residual connections let signal and gradients flow straight through, and layer normalization keeps the activations well-scaled at every depth.
This residual-and-norm sandwich is what makes very deep stacks trainable at all.
With pre-norm placement, each sub-layer reads a normalized input and adds its result back to the residual stream:
sections.texNote: The MLP is two linear layers with a nonlinearity, applied to each token independently.

sections.caption: Residual + norm around two sub-layers — repeat N times.

takeaways: A transformer is one block (attention + MLP) stacked with residuals and normalization.
Residual connections keep gradients flowing through deep stacks.
Attention mixes tokens; the MLP processes each token independently.

concepts.title: Edge Detection
concepts.oneLine: Find boundaries where image intensity changes sharply.

paras: Edges are where brightness changes fast - the outlines that carry most of an image's structure. Gradient operators like Sobel estimate that change; the Canny pipeline then thins the response and links strong, connected edges while suppressing noise. It is the front end of countless vision algorithms.
Edge strength is the gradient magnitude:
sections.texNote: Canny adds non-max suppression and hysteresis thresholding on top of this.

sections.code:
import numpy as np

Sx = np.array([[-1,0,1],[-2,0,2],[-1,0,1]])
Gx = conv2d(I, Sx); Gy = conv2d(I, Sx.T)
mag = np.hypot(Gx, Gy)            # edge strength
sections.caption: Sobel gradients give magnitude and direction.

takeaways: Edges are gradient maxima in intensity.
Sobel estimates the gradient; Canny refines it.
Edge maps front-end detection, matching, and segmentation.

concepts.title: Corner Detection
concepts.oneLine: Find points where intensity changes in every direction.

paras: Corners are the most distinctive local features - unlike a smooth region or a straight edge, a corner shifts in appearance whichever way you move. The Harris detector measures this with the structure tensor of local gradients; large change in two directions means a corner worth tracking across frames.
The Harris response from the structure tensor M:
sections.texNote: Large positive R means two strong gradient directions - a corner.

sections.code:
Ix, Iy = grad(I)
M = [[smooth(Ix*Ix), smooth(Ix*Iy)],
     [smooth(Ix*Iy), smooth(Iy*Iy)]]
R = det(M) - 0.04 * trace(M)**2      # corners where R is large
sections.caption: Two strong gradient directions = a trackable corner.

takeaways: Corners change in all directions - the best local features.
The structure tensor's eigenvalues reveal them.
They anchor tracking, matching, and motion estimation.

concepts.title: HOG Features
concepts.oneLine: Describe shape by the histogram of gradient orientations in each cell.

paras: Before deep nets, HOG was the go-to descriptor for object shape, especially pedestrians. Split the image into small cells, build a histogram of gradient orientations in each, then normalize over blocks for lighting invariance. The result is a compact vector capturing local edge structure.
Each pixel votes into orientation bins weighted by gradient magnitude:
sections.texNote: Block normalization across neighboring cells gives robustness to illumination.

sections.code:
import numpy as np
mag = np.hypot(Gx, Gy)
ori = (np.degrees(np.arctan2(Gy, Gx)) % 180)
bins = (ori / 20).astype(int)            # 9 orientation bins per cell
# accumulate mag into per-cell histograms, then block-normalize
sections.caption: Orientation histograms per cell, normalized per block.

takeaways: HOG encodes shape as per-cell gradient-orientation histograms.
Block normalization adds lighting invariance.
It powered classical detection before CNNs.

concepts.title: The Hough Transform
concepts.oneLine: Detect lines by having edge points vote in parameter space.

paras: Once you have edges, how do you find straight lines? Each edge point votes for every line that could pass through it, in a (rho, theta) accumulator. Real lines collect many votes and show up as bright peaks. It is a robust, global way to find shapes even with gaps and noise.
Each point (x, y) maps to a sinusoid of lines through it:
sections.texNote: Collinear points share a (rho, theta) cell - the peak is their common line.

sections.caption: Edge points vote; accumulator peaks are the lines.

takeaways: The Hough transform detects shapes by voting.
Collinear edges peak at one (rho, theta) cell.
It is robust to gaps and noise; it extends to circles.

concepts.title: Image Segmentation
concepts.oneLine: Partition an image into coherent regions or objects.

paras: Segmentation labels every pixel, grouping them into regions that belong together. Classical watershed treats intensity as a landscape and floods basins from markers, with boundaries forming where basins meet. It is how you separate touching objects before counting or measuring them.
Watershed floods from markers; ridges between catchment basins become boundaries:
sections.texNote: Marker placement controls over- versus under-segmentation.

sections.code:
# marker-controlled watershed (sketch)
dist = distance_transform(binary)
markers = local_maxima(dist)
labels = watershed(-dist, markers)     # basins flood from markers
sections.caption: Flood from markers; boundaries form where basins collide.

takeaways: Segmentation assigns every pixel to a region.
Watershed floods basins from markers to split touching objects.
Modern deep segmentation learns the regions end-to-end.

concepts.title: IoU and Non-Max Suppression
concepts.oneLine: Collapse many overlapping detections into clean, single boxes.

paras: A detector fires many overlapping boxes around each object. Non-max suppression keeps the highest-scoring box and discards others that overlap it too much, where overlap is measured by intersection-over-union. The same IoU metric also scores how well a predicted box matches the ground truth.
IoU is overlap area over union area:
sections.texNote: NMS removes any box with IoU above a threshold against a higher-scoring one.

sections.caption: Keep the best box, drop its high-overlap neighbors, repeat.

takeaways: IoU measures box overlap quality.
NMS deduplicates overlapping detections by score.
The IoU threshold trades duplicates against missed objects.

concepts.title: Optical Flow
concepts.oneLine: Estimate the per-pixel motion between two frames.

paras: Optical flow asks: where did each pixel go between frames? Assuming brightness is conserved as things move, the Lucas-Kanade method solves a small least-squares system in each neighborhood to recover the local motion vector. It powers tracking, stabilization, and motion-based segmentation.
The brightness-constancy constraint relates spatial and temporal gradients:
sections.texNote: One equation, two unknowns - Lucas-Kanade adds neighbors to solve it.

sections.code:
# Lucas-Kanade in a window: solve A [u v]^T = b
A = np.stack([Ix[win], Iy[win]], 1)
b = -It[win]
uv = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)[0]
sections.caption: Least-squares over a patch gives the local flow.

takeaways: Optical flow recovers per-pixel motion between frames.
Brightness constancy plus a local window makes it solvable.
It only works for small motions - hence coarse-to-fine pyramids.

concepts.title: Beam Search
concepts.oneLine: Keep several candidate continuations instead of committing greedily.

paras: Greedy decoding picks the single best next token and can paint itself into a corner. Beam search keeps the B most probable partial sequences at each step, expanding all of them and pruning back to B. It finds higher-probability sequences than greedy at B times the cost.
Score a sequence by its summed log-probability and keep the top B:
sections.texNote: Length-normalize the score, or beam search favors short sequences.

sections.caption: Expand every beam, keep the top B by score.

takeaways: Beam search tracks the top-B partial sequences.
It beats greedy on sequence probability at B times the cost.
Length normalization stops it preferring short outputs.

concepts.title: The KV Cache
concepts.oneLine: Cache past keys and values so each new token is cheap to generate.

paras: When generating text token by token, the keys and values for all previous tokens never change. Recomputing them every step is wasteful. The KV cache stores them, so producing the next token only computes one new query against the cached keys and values - turning quadratic regeneration into linear growth.
Step t attends a single new query against all cached keys and values:
sections.texNote: Only q_t is new each step; K and V are appended to and reused from the cache.

sections.code:
# generation loop with a growing cache
K_cache, V_cache = [], []
for step in range(max_len):
    q, k, v = project(next_token)
    K_cache.append(k); V_cache.append(v)
    out = attend(q, np.array(K_cache), np.array(V_cache))
sections.caption: Append the new key/value; reuse all the old ones.

takeaways: The KV cache stores past keys and values across steps.
It makes per-token generation cost grow linearly, not quadratically.
Its memory cost motivates cache eviction and paging.

concepts.title: Rotary Position Embeddings
concepts.oneLine: Encode position by rotating query and key vectors.

paras: Instead of adding a position signal, RoPE rotates each query and key by an angle proportional to its position. Because a dot product of two rotated vectors depends only on their angle difference, attention naturally sees relative position - and it extrapolates to longer contexts better than learned absolute embeddings.
Rotate by a position-dependent angle so dot products encode relative offset:
sections.tex: \langle R_{\theta m} q,\ R_{\theta n} k\rangle = g(q, k,\ m-n)
sections.texNote: The result depends on m - n, the relative position, not the absolute indices.

sections.code:
import numpy as np

def rope(x, pos, base=10000):
    d = x.shape[-1]; i = np.arange(0, d, 2)
    theta = pos / base ** (i / d)
    c, s = np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)
    return np.stack([x[..., ::2]*c - x[..., 1::2]*s,
                     x[..., ::2]*s + x[..., 1::2]*c], -1).reshape(x.shape)
sections.caption: Rotate pairs of dimensions by a position-scaled angle.

takeaways: RoPE encodes position by rotating Q and K.
Attention then sees relative position for free.
It extends to longer contexts better than absolute encodings.

concepts.title: Diffusion Models
concepts.oneLine: Add noise to data, then train a network to reverse it step by step.

paras: A diffusion model learns to denoise. The forward process gradually corrupts data into pure noise; the model learns the reverse, removing a little noise at each step. To generate, start from random noise and run the learned denoiser repeatedly until a clean sample emerges. It is the engine behind modern image generators.
The network predicts the noise added at each step, trained by a simple regression:
sections.texNote: Sampling reverses the chain: subtract the predicted noise, repeat over many steps.

sections.code:
# training step: predict the noise you added
t = np.random.randint(T)
noise = np.random.randn(*x.shape)
x_t = sqrt_acp[t]*x + sqrt_1macp[t]*noise
loss = ((noise - model(x_t, t))**2).mean()
sections.caption: Learn to predict the noise; sampling denoises from scratch.

takeaways: Diffusion learns to reverse a gradual noising process.
The objective is simple noise-prediction regression.
Generation iteratively denoises from pure noise.

concepts.title: Generative Adversarial Networks
concepts.oneLine: Train a generator against a discriminator in a minimax game.

paras: A GAN pits two networks against each other: a generator turns noise into fake samples, a discriminator tries to tell fake from real. As the discriminator improves, it pushes the generator toward more realistic output. At equilibrium the fakes are indistinguishable from real data.
The two networks play a minimax game over the discriminator's accuracy:
sections.texNote: Training is a delicate balance - if either network wins too fast, learning stalls.

sections.code:
# alternate two updates
d_loss = -(log(D(real)) + log(1 - D(G(z)))).mean()   # train D
g_loss = -log(D(G(z))).mean()                       # train G
# step D, then step G
sections.caption: Discriminator learns to judge; generator learns to fool it.

takeaways: A GAN is a generator-vs-discriminator minimax game.
Adversarial pressure drives realistic samples.
Training instability is the central challenge.

concepts.title: Variational Autoencoders
concepts.oneLine: Encode data to a distribution, sample, and decode to generate.

paras: A VAE learns a smooth latent space you can sample from. The encoder maps each input to a distribution (a mean and spread), you sample a latent code, and the decoder reconstructs the input. A regularizer keeps the latent space close to a standard Gaussian, so sampling it produces plausible new data.
Maximize the evidence lower bound: reconstruction minus a latent KL penalty:
sections.texNote: The reparameterization trick z = mu + sigma * eps lets gradients flow through sampling.

sections.code:
mu, logvar = encoder(x)
z = mu + np.exp(0.5*logvar) * np.random.randn(*mu.shape)
recon = decoder(z)
kl = -0.5 * np.sum(1 + logvar - mu**2 - np.exp(logvar))
sections.caption: Encode to a distribution, sample, decode; KL keeps it regular.

takeaways: A VAE learns a continuous, sampleable latent space.
The ELBO balances reconstruction against a latent prior.
The reparameterization trick makes sampling differentiable.

concepts.title: Contrastive Learning
concepts.oneLine: Pull matching pairs together and push mismatches apart in embedding space.

paras: Contrastive learning shapes an embedding space by example: matching pairs (two crops of an image, or an image and its caption) should land close together; everything else should be far apart. This is how CLIP aligns images and text into one space, enabling zero-shot recognition and cross-modal search.
The InfoNCE loss makes the positive pair win a softmax over negatives:
sections.texNote: tau is a temperature; the negatives are the other items in the batch.

sections.code:
# in-batch contrastive (CLIP-style)
logits = (Z_img @ Z_txt.T) / tau
labels = np.arange(len(Z_img))      # i-th image matches i-th text
loss = cross_entropy(logits, labels)
sections.caption: The diagonal pairs are positives; everything off-diagonal is negative.

takeaways: Contrastive learning aligns matching pairs in embedding space.
InfoNCE turns it into a softmax over in-batch negatives.
It powers CLIP and self-supervised representations.

concepts.title: Vector Search
concepts.oneLine: Find the nearest embeddings to a query, fast, at scale.

paras: Once everything is an embedding, retrieval becomes nearest-neighbor search: find the stored vectors closest to a query vector. Exact search is too slow at scale, so approximate methods (HNSW graphs, IVF, product quantization) trade a little accuracy for orders-of-magnitude speed. It is the backbone of RAG and semantic search.
Retrieve the top-k by similarity, usually cosine:
sections.texNote: Approximate indexes return near-neighbors in sublinear time.

sections.code:
import numpy as np

def search(q, V, k=5):
    sims = V @ q / (np.linalg.norm(V, axis=1) * np.linalg.norm(q))
    return np.argsort(sims)[::-1][:k]
sections.caption: Brute force shown; real systems use ANN indexes.

takeaways: Retrieval over embeddings is nearest-neighbor search.
Approximate indexes trade slight accuracy for big speedups.
It is the retrieval half of RAG.

concepts.title: Direct Preference Optimization
concepts.oneLine: Optimize a model on preferences directly, skipping the RL loop.

paras: RLHF trains a reward model, then runs reinforcement learning against it - powerful but finicky. DPO shows you can skip the middle step: a clever reparameterization turns the preference objective into a simple classification loss on the policy itself, tied to a frozen reference model, with no sampling or reward model needed.
DPO raises the implicit reward of chosen over rejected, anchored to a reference policy:
sections.texNote: beta controls how far the policy may drift from the reference.

sections.code:
# DPO loss: chosen y_w over rejected y_l vs a frozen reference
dw = beta * (logp(pi, y_w) - logp(ref, y_w))
dl = beta * (logp(pi, y_l) - logp(ref, y_l))
loss = -np.log(sigmoid(dw - dl)).mean()
sections.caption: A single classification loss - no reward model, no RL rollout.

takeaways: DPO optimizes preferences directly as a classification loss.
It removes the separate reward model and RL loop.
beta and the reference policy keep it from drifting.

concepts.title: LoRA
concepts.oneLine: Fine-tune with a tiny low-rank update instead of all the weights.

paras: Full fine-tuning updates every weight - expensive to train and store. LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and learns a small low-rank correction alongside them. A few million extra parameters can specialize a giant model, and you can swap adapters per task without touching the base.
Add a rank-r update B A to the frozen weight W:
sections.tex: W' = W + B A,\qquad B\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r},\; A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k},\; r\ll d
sections.texNote: Only A and B are trained; W stays frozen. Tiny, swappable, and mergeable.

sections.code:
# only A, B are trainable; W is frozen
A = np.random.randn(r, k) * 0.01
B = np.zeros((d, r))
y = x @ (W + B @ A).T          # forward uses W + BA
sections.caption: A few million low-rank parameters specialize a frozen model.

takeaways: LoRA learns a low-rank correction to frozen weights.
It cuts trainable parameters and memory by orders of magnitude.
Adapters are swappable and mergeable per task.

concepts.title: Reward Modeling
concepts.oneLine: Learn a scalar reward from human preference comparisons.

paras: You cannot write down a loss for 'a helpful answer', but people can compare two answers and say which is better. A reward model learns a scalar score from many such comparisons, so that preferred responses score higher. That learned reward is what RLHF then optimizes the policy against.
The Bradley-Terry model turns score differences into preference probabilities:
sections.texNote: Train r by maximizing the log-likelihood of the observed preferences.

sections.code:
# pairwise preference loss (chosen > rejected)
loss = -np.log(sigmoid(r(chosen) - r(rejected))).mean()
sections.caption: Push the chosen response's score above the rejected one's.

takeaways: Reward models learn from pairwise preferences, not absolute labels.
Bradley-Terry links score gaps to preference probabilities.
Goodhart risk: optimizing a proxy reward invites reward hacking.

concepts.title: Actor-Critic
concepts.oneLine: Pair a policy (actor) with a learned value baseline (critic).

paras: Pure policy gradients are noisy because returns are noisy. Actor-critic adds a critic that learns the value function and supplies a low-variance baseline, so the actor updates on the advantage - how much better an action was than expected - instead of the raw return. It is the template behind A2C, PPO, and SAC.
The actor updates on the advantage, estimated by the critic's TD error:
sections.texNote: The critic learns V; the actor ascends grad log-pi times A.

sections.code:
delta = r + gamma * V[s2] - V[s]      # TD error = advantage
V[s]   += lr_v * delta                # critic
theta  += lr_a * score(s, a) * delta  # actor
sections.caption: One TD error trains both the critic and the actor.

takeaways: Actor-critic combines a policy with a learned value baseline.
Updating on advantage cuts variance.
It underlies A2C, PPO, and SAC.

concepts.title: Multi-Armed Bandits
concepts.oneLine: The simplest RL problem: balance exploring options against exploiting the best.

paras: A bandit faces several actions with unknown payoffs and must learn which is best while earning reward. Pull the current best too eagerly and you may never discover a better one; explore too much and you waste pulls. Strategies like epsilon-greedy and UCB formalize this explore-exploit trade-off - the heart of all RL.
UCB picks the arm with the best optimistic estimate, favoring uncertain arms:
sections.texNote: The bonus term shrinks as an arm is tried more, so exploration self-regulates.

sections.caption: Optimism in the face of uncertainty.

takeaways: Bandits isolate the explore-exploit trade-off.
Epsilon-greedy explores at random; UCB explores by uncertainty.
Every RL method inherits this tension.

concepts.title: Double Q-Learning
concepts.oneLine: Cancel the optimistic bias that fools plain Q-learning.

paras: Taking a max over noisy action-value estimates systematically overestimates - the maximization bias. Double Q-learning keeps two value tables and uses one to pick the best action and the other to evaluate it, decoupling selection from evaluation so the noise no longer inflates the estimate.
Select with one estimator, evaluate with the other:
sections.texNote: Randomly update A or B each step; the cross-evaluation removes the upward bias.

sections.code:
if np.random.rand() < 0.5:
    a_star = Q_A[s2].argmax()
    Q_A[s, a] += alpha * (r + gamma * Q_B[s2, a_star] - Q_A[s, a])
# else symmetric: pick with B, evaluate with A
sections.caption: Decouple action selection from action evaluation.

takeaways: max over noisy estimates overestimates values.
Double Q-learning decouples selection from evaluation.
It is the idea behind Double DQN.

concepts.title: Deep Q-Networks
concepts.oneLine: Replace the Q-table with a network - stabilized by replay and a target net.

paras: When states are too many to tabulate (pixels, say), approximate Q with a neural network. Two tricks keep it from diverging: a replay buffer that breaks the correlation between consecutive samples, and a slowly-updated target network that provides a stable regression goal. Together they made deep RL work on Atari.
Regress the network Q toward a target built from a frozen copy:
sections.texNote: theta^- is the target network, copied from theta every so often.

sections.code:
# sample a minibatch from replay, regress to the target net
y = r + gamma * Q_target(s2).max(1) * (1 - done)
loss = ((y - Q(s).gather(a)) ** 2).mean()
sections.caption: Replay decorrelates data; the target net stabilizes the goal.

takeaways: DQN approximates Q with a neural network.
Experience replay breaks sample correlation.
A target network gives a stable regression target.

concepts.title: Dyna-Q
concepts.oneLine: Learn a model of the world and plan inside it between real steps.

paras: Real experience is expensive. Dyna-Q learns a one-step model from the transitions it sees, then between real steps it replays imagined transitions through that model, running extra Q-updates for free. A handful of planning steps per real step can slash the experience needed to solve a maze.
Each real step is followed by n planning updates on remembered transitions:
sections.texNote: More planning steps means faster learning - until the model's errors dominate.

sections.code:
model[s, a] = (r, s2)                  # learn the model
for _ in range(n):                    # plan
    (sp, ap), (rp, s2p) = sample(model)
    Q[sp, ap] += alpha * (rp + gamma * Q[s2p].max() - Q[sp, ap])
sections.caption: Act once, then imagine n more transitions.

takeaways: Dyna-Q mixes model-free learning with model-based planning.
Planning updates reuse a learned one-step model.
It is far more sample-efficient than model-free alone.

concepts.title: Generalized Advantage Estimation
concepts.oneLine: Tune the bias-variance trade-off of the advantage signal.

paras: Policy gradients need an advantage estimate: how much better was an action than expected? Use one-step TD and it is low-variance but biased by the critic; use the full return and it is unbiased but noisy. GAE blends all horizons with a decay lambda, giving a single knob to trade bias against variance.
An exponentially-weighted sum of TD residuals:
sections.texNote: lambda = 0 is one-step TD advantage; lambda = 1 is the Monte Carlo advantage.

sections.code:
adv, gae = np.zeros(T), 0.0
for t in reversed(range(T)):
    delta = r[t] + gamma * V[t+1] - V[t]
    gae = delta + gamma * lam * gae
    adv[t] = gae
sections.caption: A backward pass blends every horizon's TD error.

takeaways: GAE trades advantage bias against variance with lambda.
It is computed in one backward pass over a trajectory.
It is the standard advantage estimator inside PPO.

concepts.title: MDPs and the Bellman Equation
concepts.oneLine: Frame sequential decisions, and solve them with a recursive value identity.

paras: A Markov decision process is states, actions, rewards, and transitions. The value of a state is the best total reward you can expect from it. The Bellman equation makes this recursive: a state's value is the immediate reward plus the discounted value of where you land next - which value iteration solves by repeated backups.
The optimal value satisfies the Bellman optimality equation:
sections.texNote: gamma discounts the future; iterating this backup converges to V*.

sections.caption: Repeated backups converge to the optimal values.

takeaways: MDPs formalize sequential decision-making.
Bellman makes value recursive: reward now plus discounted value next.
Value iteration solves a known MDP by repeated backups.

concepts.title: Policy Gradients
concepts.oneLine: Optimize the policy directly by following the gradient of expected reward.

paras: Instead of learning values and acting greedily, policy gradients adjust the policy's parameters to make high-reward actions more likely. REINFORCE nudges the log-probability of each action by the return that followed it. It handles continuous actions naturally but can be high-variance.
The policy-gradient theorem weights each action's log-prob gradient by its return:
sections.texNote: Subtracting a baseline from G_t cuts variance without adding bias.

sections.code:
# REINFORCE update over a trajectory
for (s, a, G) in trajectory:
    grad = score(s, a)             # d log pi(a|s)/d theta
    theta += lr * grad * (G - baseline)
sections.caption: Make actions that led to high return more likely.

takeaways: Policy gradients optimize the policy directly.
REINFORCE scales each log-prob gradient by its return.
A baseline reduces variance without bias.

concepts.title: Proximal Policy Optimization
concepts.oneLine: Take the biggest safe policy step by clipping the update.

paras: Big policy-gradient steps can collapse a policy. PPO lets you reuse a batch for several updates but clips the change in action probabilities, so the new policy never strays too far from the old one. This simple clip makes training stable and sample-efficient - it is the default for RLHF.
Clip the probability ratio so the surrogate objective cannot reward going too far:
sections.texNote: r_t is the new/old probability ratio; outside the band the gradient is zero.

sections.code:
ratio = np.exp(logp_new - logp_old)
clip = np.clip(ratio, 1 - eps, 1 + eps)
loss = -np.minimum(ratio * A, clip * A).mean()
sections.caption: The clip parks the ratio inside a trust region.

takeaways: PPO clips the policy update into a trust region.
It allows several epochs per batch, stably.
It is the workhorse of modern RL and RLHF.

concepts.title: Q-Learning
concepts.oneLine: Learn action-values from experience, without knowing the environment.

paras: When you do not know the transition model, you learn from samples. Q-learning estimates the value of each action in each state, nudging its estimate toward the observed reward plus the best next-state value. It is off-policy: it learns the optimal policy even while exploring with a different one.
The temporal-difference update on the action-value Q:
sections.texNote: The bracket is the TD error - the surprise that drives learning.

sections.code:
td = r + gamma * Q[s2].max() - Q[s, a]
Q[s, a] += alpha * td
sections.caption: Move the estimate toward reward plus best next value.

takeaways: Q-learning is model-free, off-policy value learning.
The TD error is the learning signal.
max over next actions makes it learn the greedy optimum.

concepts.title: SARSA
concepts.oneLine: On-policy control: update toward the action you actually took.

paras: SARSA is Q-learning's on-policy twin. Where Q-learning bootstraps from the best next action, SARSA bootstraps from the action its policy actually chose next - so it learns the value of the policy it is following, exploration and all. On a cliff-edge task it learns the safe path; Q-learning learns the risky optimal one.
The target uses the next action a' sampled from the current policy:
sections.texNote: Replace Q(s',a') with max over a' and you are back to Q-learning.

sections.code:
a2 = policy(s2)                       # on-policy: sample next action
Q[s, a] += alpha * (r + gamma * Q[s2, a2] - Q[s, a])
sections.caption: Bootstrap from the action the policy really takes.

takeaways: SARSA is on-policy: it values the policy it follows.
Q-learning is off-policy: it values the greedy optimum.
On-policy learning is safer under exploration.

concepts.title: TD(lambda) and Eligibility Traces
concepts.oneLine: Dial smoothly between one-step TD and full Monte Carlo.

paras: One-step TD updates from the very next reward (low variance, biased); Monte Carlo waits for the full return (unbiased, high variance). TD(lambda) blends them with eligibility traces - a fading memory of recently visited states - so one update credits a whole trajectory. Intermediate lambda often learns fastest.
The trace decays by gamma*lambda and gates how much each state is updated:
sections.texNote: lambda = 0 is one-step TD; lambda = 1 is Monte Carlo.

sections.code:
delta = r + gamma * V[s2] - V[s]
e[s] += 1                              # mark visited
V += alpha * delta * e                 # update all eligible states
e *= gamma * lam                       # decay the trace
sections.caption: One TD error updates every recently-seen state.

takeaways: Eligibility traces credit a whole trajectory per step.
lambda interpolates TD(0) and Monte Carlo.
Intermediate lambda usually learns fastest.

concepts.title: Autograd and the Computational Graph
concepts.oneLine: How a framework records operations and replays them backward for gradients.

paras: PyTorch's autograd builds a graph as you compute: every tensor operation records its inputs and how to backpropagate through it. Calling .backward() walks that graph in reverse, applying the chain rule at each node, and deposits a gradient on every leaf tensor. You never write a derivative by hand.
Reverse-mode autodiff accumulates the gradient through each recorded op:
sections.texNote: Each op knows its local Jacobian-vector product; autograd chains them.

sections.code:
x = torch.tensor([2.0], requires_grad=True)
y = (x ** 2 + 3 * x).sum()
y.backward()          # walks the graph in reverse
print(x.grad)         # dy/dx = 2x + 3 = 7
sections.caption: Build the graph forward; differentiate it backward, automatically.

takeaways: Autograd records a graph of operations as you compute.
.backward() applies the chain rule in reverse over that graph.
Frameworks free you from writing derivatives by hand.

concepts.title: The Training Loop
concepts.oneLine: The five-line skeleton at the heart of every training script.

paras: Strip away the abstractions and every PyTorch training run is the same loop: get a batch, run the forward pass, compute the loss, backpropagate, and step the optimizer. Everything else - schedulers, logging, checkpoints, mixed precision - hangs off this skeleton.
Each iteration is one minibatch gradient-descent step:
sections.texNote: The minibatch B gives a noisy but cheap gradient estimate.

sections.code:
for x, y in loader:
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = criterion(model(x), y)   # forward + loss
    loss.backward()                 # gradients
    opt.step()                      # update
sections.caption: Batch, forward, loss, backward, step - repeat.

takeaways: Every training script is this five-line loop.
Minibatches give cheap, noisy gradient estimates.
Schedulers, logging, and checkpoints decorate this skeleton.

concepts.title: The Optimizer Step
concepts.oneLine: How torch.optim turns accumulated gradients into a weight update.

paras: After backward fills in the gradients, an optimizer object applies the update rule. It holds the parameters and any per-parameter state (like Adam's moment estimates), and .step() applies the rule while .zero_grad() clears the gradients for the next iteration. Swapping SGD for Adam is a one-line change.
The optimizer applies its update rule to each parameter using its stored state:
sections.texNote: u is the rule (SGD, Adam, ...); state carries momentum and scale across steps.

sections.code:
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4)
# each iteration:
opt.zero_grad()       # clear old grads
loss.backward()       # fill grads
opt.step()            # apply the update rule
sections.caption: zero_grad, backward, step - the same three calls every iteration.

takeaways: The optimizer owns the parameters and their update state.
.step() applies the rule; .zero_grad() resets gradients.
Changing optimizers is a one-line swap.

concepts.title: Gradient Clipping
concepts.oneLine: Cap the gradient norm so a bad batch cannot blow up training.

paras: Occasionally a batch produces a huge gradient that sends the weights flying and the loss to NaN - common in RNNs and transformers. Clipping rescales the gradient when its norm exceeds a threshold, preserving direction but bounding the step. Cheap insurance against rare instabilities.
Rescale the gradient if its norm exceeds the threshold c:
sections.texNote: Direction is preserved; only the magnitude is capped.

sections.caption: Keep the direction, bound the magnitude.

takeaways: Clipping bounds the update from a rare huge gradient.
It preserves direction, only scaling magnitude.
Standard practice for RNNs and transformers.

concepts.title: Learning-Rate Schedules
concepts.oneLine: Vary the step size over training - warm up, then decay.

paras: A fixed learning rate is a compromise. Schedules do better: a short warmup avoids early instability while statistics settle, then a decay (cosine or linear) lets the model settle into a good minimum. The right schedule can matter as much as the optimizer.
A cosine schedule decays smoothly from the peak rate to near zero:
sections.texNote: Often preceded by a linear warmup over the first few percent of steps.

sections.caption: Warm up, then cosine-decay to near zero.

takeaways: Schedules beat a single fixed learning rate.
Warmup avoids early divergence; decay sharpens the minimum.
Cosine decay is a strong default.

concepts.title: Mixed Precision
concepts.oneLine: Train in 16-bit for speed and memory, with safeguards for accuracy.

paras: Half-precision (fp16 / bf16) halves memory and runs far faster on modern hardware, but fp16's narrow range can underflow small gradients to zero. Mixed precision keeps a master copy of the weights in fp32 and scales the loss up before the backward pass so gradients stay representable, then scales them back down.
Loss scaling shifts gradients into fp16's representable range:
sections.texNote: Scale up by S before backward, unscale by S after - bf16's wider range often skips this.

sections.code:
scaled_loss = loss * S            # S ~ 2^14
scaled_loss.backward()
grads = [g / S for g in grads]    # unscale before the step
sections.caption: Compute in 16-bit, accumulate the master weights in 32-bit.

takeaways: fp16 / bf16 cut memory and speed up training.
Loss scaling stops fp16 gradients underflowing.
An fp32 master copy preserves accuracy.

concepts.title: Scaling Laws
concepts.oneLine: Loss falls as a predictable power law in compute, data, and parameters.

paras: Model quality improves smoothly and predictably with scale. Empirically, test loss drops as a power law in parameters, data, and compute - straight lines on a log-log plot. These curves let you forecast a big model's loss from small runs and allocate a compute budget optimally between size and data.
Loss versus a scale factor N follows a power law:
sections.texNote: Compute-optimal training (Chinchilla) balances N and data D for a fixed budget.

sections.code:
import numpy as np
# fit a power law to small-scale runs, extrapolate
logL = np.log(losses); logN = np.log(sizes)
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(logN, logL, 1)   # slope = -alpha
sections.caption: A line on a log-log plot predicts the next scale.

takeaways: Loss is a power law in compute, data, and parameters.
Small runs forecast large ones.
Compute-optimal training balances model size against data.

concepts.title: Knowledge Distillation
concepts.oneLine: Train a small student to mimic a big teacher's soft predictions.

paras: A big model's full probability distribution carries more information than a hard label - the relative scores of the wrong classes encode 'dark knowledge'. Distillation trains a small student to match the teacher's softened outputs, transferring much of the teacher's skill into a fraction of the size.
Match softened teacher and student distributions at temperature T:
sections.texNote: High T exposes the dark knowledge in the teacher's non-top classes.

sections.code:
soft_t = softmax(teacher_logits / T)
soft_s = softmax(student_logits / T)
loss = (1-a)*ce(y, student_logits) + a*T*T*kl(soft_t, soft_s)
sections.caption: Learn from the teacher's whole distribution, not just the label.

takeaways: Distillation transfers a teacher's soft predictions to a student.
Dark knowledge lives in the non-top class probabilities.
Temperature controls how much of it is exposed.

concepts.title: Mixture of Experts
concepts.oneLine: Route each token to a few specialist sub-networks, not all of them.

paras: A dense layer runs every parameter on every token. A mixture of experts has many expert sub-networks and a router that sends each token to just the top few. The model holds enormous total capacity, but each token only activates a slice of it - so quality scales with parameters while compute stays roughly fixed.
A router picks the top-k experts per token and mixes their outputs by gate weight:
sections.texNote: A load-balancing loss keeps the router from collapsing onto a few experts.

sections.code:
gate = softmax(router @ x)           # scores over experts
topk = gate.argsort()[-k:]           # pick k experts
y = sum(gate[e] * expert[e](x) for e in topk)
sections.caption: Only the top-k experts run per token.

takeaways: MoE activates only a few experts per token.
Total capacity grows while per-token compute stays fixed.
Load balancing prevents router collapse.

concepts.title: Paged Attention
concepts.oneLine: Manage the KV cache like virtual memory to kill fragmentation.

paras: Serving many requests with different lengths fragments the KV-cache memory, wasting much of the GPU. Paged attention borrows the OS idea of paging: store the cache in fixed-size blocks allocated on demand, so memory is packed tightly and sequences can share blocks. It is what lets servers batch far more requests.
A logical token position maps to a physical block and offset:
sections.texNote: Non-contiguous blocks via an indirection table - just like OS page tables.

sections.code:
# a block table maps logical positions to physical blocks
block = block_table[seq][i // B]
k = kv_blocks[block][i % B]            # gather K/V by page
sections.caption: Fixed-size pages, allocated on demand, packed tight.

takeaways: Paged attention pages the KV cache like virtual memory.
It removes fragmentation and packs more requests per GPU.
It is the core idea behind high-throughput servers like vLLM.

concepts.title: Pruning
concepts.oneLine: Remove the weights that barely matter to shrink the model.

paras: Most weights in a trained network contribute little. Magnitude pruning zeros the smallest ones, and a brief retrain lets the survivors compensate. Accuracy holds steady as sparsity rises, then falls off a cliff - the trick is finding that edge. Structured pruning removes whole channels for real speedups.
Keep only weights above a magnitude threshold:
sections.texNote: tau is set to hit a target sparsity; retrain after pruning to recover accuracy.

sections.code:
import numpy as np
thr = np.quantile(np.abs(W), sparsity)   # e.g. 0.8 -> drop 80%
W = W * (np.abs(W) > thr)                 # then fine-tune
sections.caption: Zero the small weights, retrain the rest.

takeaways: Pruning removes low-magnitude weights.
Accuracy holds then drops sharply past a sparsity edge.
Structured pruning yields real hardware speedups.

concepts.title: Quantization
concepts.oneLine: Store and compute weights in fewer bits with minimal accuracy loss.

paras: A model in 16-bit floats is mostly empty precision. Quantization maps weights to low-bit integers (8-bit, even 4-bit), shrinking memory and speeding up math. The trick is choosing a scale per group of weights so the rounding error stays small, and handling outliers that would otherwise stretch the scale.
Symmetric quantization rounds to a grid set by a per-group scale s:
sections.texNote: Smaller groups and outlier handling keep the reconstruction error low.

sections.caption: Round to a grid; dequantize by multiplying back.

takeaways: Quantization trades precision for memory and speed.
Per-group scales keep rounding error small.
Outliers are the main accuracy challenge.

concepts.title: Speculative Decoding
concepts.oneLine: Draft several tokens with a small model, verify them with the big one.

paras: Generation is slow because the big model runs once per token. Speculative decoding has a cheap draft model propose several tokens at once; the big model then checks them all in a single parallel pass and accepts the longest correct prefix. It is exactly as accurate as the big model, just faster.
Accept a drafted token with a probability that preserves the target distribution:
sections.texNote: A correction step on rejection makes the output identical in distribution to the target.

sections.code:
draft = small.generate(ctx, k=4)           # propose k tokens
p = big.logprobs(ctx, draft)               # verify in one pass
accept = longest_prefix_where(p_ratio >= u) # keep correct prefix
sections.caption: Propose cheaply, verify in parallel, keep the correct prefix.

takeaways: Speculative decoding drafts cheap, verifies expensive.
Output is identical in distribution to the big model.
Speedup depends on how often drafts are accepted.

concepts.title: Guardrails
concepts.oneLine: Filter inputs and outputs to keep an LLM system safe.

paras: A deployed model needs a safety pipeline around it. Input guards strip or flag prompt injection and sensitive data; output guards catch unsafe content, leaked secrets, or off-policy responses before they reach the user. Each guard is a focused check; turning one off lets the matching threat through.
The system passes only if every guard passes:
sections.texNote: Layered, independent checks - defense in depth, not a single classifier.

sections.code:
def guarded(prompt):
    if injection(prompt) or has_pii(prompt): return BLOCK
    out = model(sanitize(prompt))
    if toxic(out) or leaks_secret(out): return BLOCK
    return out
sections.caption: Check the input, generate, then check the output.

takeaways: Guardrails wrap the model with input and output checks.
Layered, independent guards give defense in depth.
Removing a guard exposes exactly its threat class.

concepts.title: HyDE
concepts.oneLine: Retrieve with a hypothetical answer instead of the raw question.

paras: A question and its answer often look different in embedding space, so querying with the question can miss the right passage. HyDE first has the model write a hypothetical answer, embeds that, and retrieves with it - because a guessed answer, even if imperfect, sits much closer to the real supporting documents.
Retrieve against the embedding of a generated answer h, not the query q:
sections.texNote: Averaging several hypothetical answers smooths out any single bad guess.

sections.code:
h = llm(f'Write a passage answering: {q}')   # hypothetical doc
hits = vector_search(embed(h), k=5)          # retrieve with it
sections.caption: Guess an answer, retrieve what supports it.

takeaways: HyDE bridges the query-document embedding gap.
It retrieves with a generated answer, not the question.
Averaging multiple drafts reduces variance.

concepts.title: Prompt Injection
concepts.oneLine: The attacks that hijack an LLM, and the layered defenses against them.

paras: Because an LLM cannot fully separate instructions from data, attacker-controlled text - in a prompt, a retrieved document, or a tool result - can override your instructions. Defenses layer up: delimit and spotlight untrusted content, assert an instruction hierarchy, classify inputs, and filter outputs for exfiltration. No single layer is sufficient.
Residual risk is what survives every defense layer:
sections.texNote: ASR is attack success rate; each defense d_l catches some fraction, none all.

sections.code:
# spotlighting: clearly fence untrusted content
prompt = (system + '
<<UNTRUSTED>>
' + retrieved + '
<<END>>')
# plus an output filter that blocks secret/exfiltration patterns
sections.caption: Defense in depth - delimit, prioritize, classify, filter.

takeaways: Injection exploits the instruction-vs-data ambiguity.
Untrusted text can arrive via documents and tool results.
Layered defenses reduce, but never zero, the attack surface.

concepts.title: Chunking for Retrieval
concepts.oneLine: Split documents so the answer survives retrieval intact.

paras: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a model in your documents - but only if the right passage is retrievable. Chunking decides how documents are split into embeddable units. Too large and a chunk dilutes the relevant sentence; too small and it loses context. Overlap and sentence-aware boundaries keep answers from being cut in half.
Retrieve the top chunks by similarity to the query embedding:
sections.texNote: Chunk size and overlap control whether the answer span lands inside one retrieved chunk.

sections.caption: Sliding windows with overlap keep answer spans whole.

takeaways: Chunking sets what retrieval can actually find.
Size and overlap trade context against precision.
Sentence-aware splits avoid cutting answers in half.

concepts.title: The ReAct Agent Loop
concepts.oneLine: Interleave reasoning with tool calls in a thought-action-observation loop.

paras: A ReAct agent alternates thinking and acting: it reasons about what to do, calls a tool, observes the result, and repeats until it can answer. Tools (search, a calculator, code) let it ground its reasoning in real results instead of hallucinating - but every step is a chance to go off the rails, so reliability compounds.
End-to-end success is the product of per-step reliability:
sections.texNote: Many steps at 0.9 each still fail often - hence verification and retries.

sections.code:
while not done:
    thought = model(scratchpad)            # reason
    action, arg = parse_tool(thought)      # act
    obs = tools[action](arg)               # observe
    scratchpad += f'{thought}\n{obs}\n'
sections.caption: Thought, action, observation - loop until answered.

takeaways: ReAct interleaves reasoning with grounded tool calls.
Tools curb hallucination by injecting real results.
Per-step error compounds, so reliability is the hard part.

concepts.title: Reflection
concepts.oneLine: Draft, critique, and revise toward a quality bar.

paras: A model can often improve its own output if asked to critique it. Reflection loops draft -> critique -> revise until a quality bar is met. The catch: self-correction is only as good as the critic. A sharp critic converges fast; a weak or miscalibrated one can pass bad answers or reject good ones.
Quality improves only when the critic carries real signal:
sections.texNote: Bounded by the verifier: a useless critic yields no gain.

sections.code:
draft = llm(task)
for _ in range(max_iters):
    critique = llm(f'Critique: {draft}')
    if passes(critique): break
    draft = llm(f'Revise given: {critique}\n{draft}')
sections.caption: Iterate until the critic is satisfied - or you give up.

takeaways: Reflection is a draft-critique-revise loop.
Its ceiling is the quality of the critic.
It is the sequential cousin of self-consistency.

concepts.title: Reranking
concepts.oneLine: Re-score the top retrieved hits with a more careful model.

paras: Fast vector search uses a bi-encoder that embeds query and document separately - cheap but coarse. A reranker is a cross-encoder that reads the query and a candidate together, scoring relevance far more accurately. You retrieve many cheaply, then rerank the top few expensively: the best of both.
A cross-encoder scores the query-document pair jointly:
sections.texNote: Joint encoding captures interactions a separate-embedding bi-encoder misses.

sections.code:
cands = vector_search(q, k=50)          # cheap recall
scores = [cross_encoder(q, d) for d in cands]
top = [cands[i] for i in argsort(scores)[::-1][:5]]
sections.caption: Retrieve broadly, rerank the shortlist precisely.

takeaways: Bi-encoders retrieve fast; cross-encoders rerank accurately.
Retrieve many, rerank a few - the standard two-stage pipeline.
Reranking sharply improves the final context quality.

concepts.title: Self-Consistency
concepts.oneLine: Sample several reasoning paths and take the majority answer.

paras: A single chain of reasoning can go wrong by chance. Self-consistency samples several independent chains at nonzero temperature and votes on the final answer. When errors are independent, the majority is far more reliable than any one path - a Condorcet-style lift. It fails when the errors are correlated.
With independent per-sample accuracy p, the majority of N improves sharply:
sections.texNote: Correlated errors break the independence this relies on.

sections.code:
from collections import Counter
answers = [extract(llm(prompt, temperature=0.7)) for _ in range(N)]
final = Counter(answers).most_common(1)[0][0]   # vote
sections.caption: Many samples, one vote - reliability from diversity.

takeaways: Self-consistency votes over multiple reasoning samples.
Independent errors make the majority much more reliable.
Correlated errors defeat it.

concepts.title: Calibration
concepts.oneLine: Make a model's confidence match its real accuracy.

paras: A trustworthy classifier that says 90% should be right about 90% of the time. Modern networks are often overconfident. Calibration fixes the scores without changing the ranking - temperature scaling divides the logits by a single learned constant so the confidences line up with observed accuracy.
Temperature scaling softens the logits by a learned scalar T:
sections.texNote: T > 1 reduces overconfidence; it is fit on validation data and leaves the argmax unchanged.

sections.code:
# fit T to minimize validation NLL; predictions unchanged in rank
p = softmax(logits / T)
ece = expected_calibration_error(p, labels)
sections.caption: One scalar recalibrates every confidence.

takeaways: Calibration aligns confidence with actual accuracy.
Temperature scaling fixes it with a single constant.
It changes confidences but not the predicted class.

concepts.title: Conformal Prediction
concepts.oneLine: Output prediction sets with a guaranteed coverage rate.

paras: Instead of one guess, conformal prediction returns a set that contains the truth with a chosen probability - say 90% - and that guarantee holds for any model, with no distributional assumptions. When the model is unsure the set is large; when it is confident the set shrinks. It turns any predictor into one with honest uncertainty.
Use a calibration quantile of nonconformity scores to build the set:
sections.texNote: Coverage of at least 1 - alpha holds marginally; set size grows as the model weakens.

sections.code:
import numpy as np
scores = nonconformity(calib_X, calib_y)
qhat = np.quantile(scores, 1 - alpha)        # threshold
pred_set = [y for y in classes if score(x, y) <= qhat]
sections.caption: Calibrate a threshold; include every plausible label.

takeaways: Conformal sets guarantee coverage for any model.
Set size grows when the model is uncertain.
Coverage is distribution-free and finite-sample valid.

concepts.title: Fairness Metrics
concepts.oneLine: Measure group disparities - and confront their impossibility.

paras: A model can be accurate yet unfair across groups. Different metrics formalize fairness: demographic parity (equal positive rates), equal opportunity (equal true-positive rates), equalized odds (both error rates equal). The uncomfortable result is that, when base rates differ, you cannot satisfy them all at once - fairness requires a choice.
Equal opportunity demands matched true-positive rates across groups:
sections.tex: P(\hat{y}=1\mid y=1, A=a) = P(\hat{y}=1\mid y=1, A=b)
sections.texNote: Demographic parity and calibration generally cannot hold simultaneously with this.

sections.code:
tpr = lambda g: ((pred==1) & (y==1) & (A==g)).sum() / ((y==1)&(A==g)).sum()
eo_gap = abs(tpr('a') - tpr('b'))      # equal-opportunity gap
sections.caption: Compute per-group rates; the gaps are the disparities.

takeaways: Fairness has several incompatible definitions.
With unequal base rates you cannot satisfy them all.
Choosing a metric is a value judgment, not a technicality.

concepts.title: Time-Series Forecasting
concepts.oneLine: Predict future values from the patterns in past observations.

paras: Forecasting exploits structure in time: trend, seasonality, and autocorrelation. Classical methods decompose the series and extrapolate; modern ones learn the patterns directly. The cardinal rule is to respect time when you evaluate - never let the model peek at the future, and backtest on rolling windows.
A series is often modeled as trend plus seasonality plus noise:
sections.texNote: Validate with rolling-origin backtests, never a random split.

sections.caption: Beat this baseline before trusting anything fancier.

takeaways: Forecasting models trend, seasonality, and autocorrelation.
Evaluate with rolling backtests, never a random split.
Always compare against a seasonal-naive baseline.

concepts.title: Explainability with SHAP
concepts.oneLine: Attribute a prediction fairly across its input features.

paras: Why did the model decide this? SHAP answers by borrowing from game theory: treat features as players and the prediction as a payout, then give each feature its Shapley value - its average marginal contribution across all orderings. It is the unique attribution that is fair and adds up to the prediction.
The Shapley value averages a feature's marginal contribution over all coalitions:
sections.texNote: The contributions sum exactly to the prediction minus the baseline.

sections.code:
# exact Shapley by enumerating coalitions (small feature sets)
from itertools import combinations
# phi_i = average of f(S + i) - f(S) over all subsets S not containing i
sections.caption: Average marginal contribution over every feature ordering.

takeaways: SHAP gives each feature its fair share of the prediction.
Attributions sum to the prediction minus a baseline.
It is the game-theoretic standard for local explanations.

concepts.title: Autoscaling
concepts.oneLine: Track demand by adding and removing replicas automatically.

paras: Traffic rises and falls; a fixed fleet either wastes money or breaks under load. An autoscaler watches a signal like utilization and adjusts the replica count toward a target. The catch is cold starts: new replicas take time to warm up, so spikes can breach the SLO before capacity catches up.
The desired replica count chases the load toward a target utilization:
sections.texNote: Lower target utilization buys headroom for spikes, at higher cost.

sections.code:
desired = ceil(load / (target_util * cap_per_replica))
replicas = clamp(desired, min_r, max_r)   # cold start adds lag
sections.caption: Scale toward a utilization target, bounded by limits.

takeaways: Autoscaling matches replicas to demand.
Target utilization trades headroom against cost.
Cold starts cause SLO breaches on sudden spikes.

concepts.title: Canary Rollouts
concepts.oneLine: Ship a new model to a slice of traffic, watch, then ramp or roll back.

paras: Deploying a new model to everyone at once is risky. A canary sends a small fraction of traffic to the new version, compares its error rate against the old one with a statistical test, and only ramps up if it passes. A regression hits a few percent of users instead of all of them, and rolls back automatically.
A one-sided test gates each ramp stage on the error-rate difference:
sections.texNote: Pass the guard, ramp the traffic split; fail, roll back.

sections.caption: Ramp the split only while the guard holds.

takeaways: Canaries limit a bad deploy's blast radius.
A statistical guard decides ramp versus rollback.
Progressive traffic shifting makes releases safe.

concepts.title: Drift Detection
concepts.oneLine: Notice when production data has shifted away from training.

paras: Models silently decay when the world changes - new user behavior, a shifted input distribution, a broken upstream feature. Drift detection compares the live input distribution against a training reference and raises an alarm when they diverge, so you retrain before accuracy quietly collapses.
The population stability index sums the binned distribution shift:
sections.texNote: PSI above ~0.2 flags a meaningful shift worth investigating.

sections.caption: Bin both distributions; sum the divergence.

takeaways: Drift detection compares live data to a training reference.
PSI quantifies distribution shift; ~0.2 is a common alarm.
Catching drift early triggers retraining before accuracy falls.

concepts.title: Serving and Batching
concepts.oneLine: Trade a little latency for far more throughput by batching requests.

paras: A served model spends most of its time idle between requests. Dynamic batching waits a few milliseconds to gather several requests and runs them together, amortizing the fixed cost and multiplying throughput. The knob is the batch window: bigger batches mean higher throughput but more tail latency.
By Little's law, queue length ties throughput to latency:
sections.texNote: Push arrival rate lambda past capacity and the queue - and latency W - runs away.

sections.code:
# accumulate until full or the window elapses, then run once
batch = collect(max_size=32, max_wait_ms=5)
results = model(batch)        # one padded forward for many requests
sections.caption: Wait briefly, batch, run once - amortize the fixed cost.

takeaways: Batching amortizes fixed cost into higher throughput.
The batch window trades throughput against tail latency.
Arrivals past capacity make the queue run away.
